module_title: Discharge, Doctrine of Frustration, Quasi-Contracts & Damages
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores how contracts come to an end. It delves into the Doctrine of Frustration, the equitable principle of Quasi-Contracts, and the landmark rules for calculating damages in case of a breach.

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Frustration (Section 56)
core_concepts.description:
Also known as 'Impossibility of Performance'. If an act becomes impossible or unlawful *after* the contract is made (due to an event the promisor could not prevent), the contract becomes void.
- Grounds for Frustration: Destruction of subject matter, death or personal incapacity, declaration of war, change of law.
- Exclusions: Commercial hardship, strikes, or self-induced impossibility do NOT amount to frustration.
- Landmark Case: *Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1954)* - The Supreme Court ruled that 'impossible' does not mean physical/literal impossibility, but rather that the object/purpose of the contract has been totally upset.

core_concepts.title: Quasi-Contracts (Sections 68-72)
core_concepts.description:
These are not actual contracts because there is no offer and acceptance. They are obligations created by law (imposed by the court) to prevent **'Unjust Enrichment'** (nobody should enrich themselves at the expense of another).
- Example (Sec 70): Obligation of a person enjoying the benefit of a non-gratuitous act. If a deliveryman mistakenly leaves a pizza at your door, and you eat it, the law imposes a Quasi-Contract on you to pay the deliveryman.

core_concepts.title: Breach of Contract & Damages (Section 73)
core_concepts.description:
When a party breaks the contract, the injured party is entitled to compensation for any loss or damage that naturally arose in the usual course of things.
- The Rule in *Hadley v. Baxendale (1854)*: Damages are awarded for (1) Ordinary/Direct losses (which arise naturally), and (2) Special losses, ONLY IF the special circumstances were communicated to the breaching party at the time of making the contract.
- Remote, indirect, or unforeseeable damages are NOT recoverable.

core_concepts.title: Liquidated Damages vs. Penalty (Section 74)
core_concepts.description:
If a contract pre-decides the penalty for a breach (e.g., 'If you delay construction, you pay 1 Lakh per day'):
- English Law differentiates between genuine pre-estimates (Liquidated Damages - allowable) and excessive threats (Penalty - void).
- Indian Law (Sec 74) ignores this distinction. The court will simply award 'reasonable compensation' not exceeding the amount named in the contract, regardless of whether it is called a penalty or liquidated damages.

important_entities.name: Novation (Section 62)
important_entities.key_fact: Substituting an old contract with a new one.
important_entities.significance: Under Discharge by Agreement, Novation occurs when parties mutually agree to substitute a new contract for the old one. Once novation occurs, the original contract need not be performed. Note: Novation can involve a change in parties.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Do not confuse Initial Impossibility with the Doctrine of Frustration. An agreement to do an act impossible *in itself* (e.g., discovering treasure by magic) is void from the beginning (Sec 56 Para 1). The Doctrine of Frustration (Sec 56 Para 2) applies to **Subsequent/Supervening Impossibility**—events that occur *after* the valid contract is formed.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: N F N F M (Necessaries 68, Finder of Goods 71, Non-gratuitous 70, Fraud/Mistake 72)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember these are purely based on equity and good conscience, not mutual consent.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC Mains or Judiciary question asks 'Explain the rules for the measurement of damages in a breach of contract', you MUST cite the twin rules of **Hadley v. Baxendale** and refer to **Section 73** of the Indian Contract Act.
